references.text: The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to get rid of Jesus (Luke 22:2). Judas's search for a suitable opportunity to betray him was a direct follow-up to their plan.

Satan entered Judas, and he went to the chief priests and the captains and arranged to hand over Jesus (Luke 22:3-5). Verse 6 is the immediate continuation where Judas agrees and begins to look for an opportunity.
Matthew's parallel account of Judas going to the chief priests and asking what they would give him to betray Jesus, and then seeking an opportunity to betray him (Matthew 26:14-16).
Mark's parallel account where Judas Iscariot went to the chief priests to betray Jesus, and they promised him money. Then he sought a suitable opportunity (Mark 14:10-11).
John confirms that the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray Jesus (John 13:2), which aligns with Judas's active search for an opportunity.

The psalmist's complaint that a close friend lifted his heel against him (Psalm 41:10). Judas's betrayal—seeking an opportunity to hand over Jesus in secret, away from the crowd—is a fulfillment of this prophetic image.
Judas Iscariot is identified early on as the one who became the betrayer (Luke 6:16). His search for a suitable opportunity in 22:6 is the culmination of that role.

Peter speaks about how Scripture had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus, even though he was counted among the twelve (Acts 1:16-17). This points back to Judas's action of seeking an opportunity to hand over Jesus.
Judas finally found the opportunity he had been seeking: he led a crowd to Jesus and betrayed him with a kiss (Luke 22:47-48), and this happened away from the crowd, just as he had planned.
